results.title: ML Reproducibility Tools and Best Practices | A minimal Hugo website
results.content: A recurrent challenge in machine learning research is to ensure that the presented and published results are reliable, robust, and reproducible [4,5,6,7]. Reproducibility, obtaining similar results as presented in a paper using the same code and data, is necessary to verify the reliability of research findings. Reproducibility is also an important step to promote open and accessible research, thereby allowing the scientific community to quickly integrate new findings and convert ideas to practice. In this blog post, we will share commonly used tools and explain 12 basic practices that you can use in your research to ensure reproducible science. Pytorch Lightning provides a great way to log all hyperparameters in `.csv` files in the experiment output folder, allowing for better reproducibility. Managing your model checkpoints is very important in terms of reproducibility, as it allows you to release trained models for the community to easily verify your work, as well as build upon it. Logging is also important for reproducibility, so researchers can verify the training progression of their replications in great detail. Probably the most important aspect of the exact reproducibility of your research is the seed of the experiment. Although exact reproducibility is not guaranteed, especially in GPU execution environments [2, 8], it’s still beneficial to report the seed due to its impact on your results. Before beginning your experiments, randomly draw \(n\) seeds and set them aside in your config file, and report all experimental results aggregated over those \(n\) seeds. When reporting your results, it is ideal to run your experiments in different seeds and/or different datasets. A higher bar of reproducibility is to report the results on *multiple datasets* to highlight the robustness of your model. While reporting your results, consult the ML Reproducibility Checklist which has detailed guidelines on the best practices for reporting figures and tables. You can also leverage headless virtual machines such as Docker or Singularity to provide the exact reproducible dev environment used for the experiments. This not only encourages reproducible research but also adds more visibility to your paper. Finally, it’s important from the reproducibility perspective to test your implementation in a *different environment* than the training setup.

results.title: Evaluating Container Security and Reproducibility in Research Software Engineering
results.content: However, research containers often include outdated or unnec-essary packages, introducing significant security vulnerabilities that conflict with reproducibility requirements. We design a reproducibility-aware DevSecOps pipeline that scans, hardens, and tests container images using best practices such as SBOM generation, minimal base images, and DockerSlim optimization. Prominent open-source scanners include Trivy [4], known for its speed and ease of integration into CI/CD pipelines; Anchore Engine [5], which offers centralized inspection and policy-based analysis, including the generation of Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs); and Clair [6], recognized for its thorough static analysis of image layers against multiple vulnerability feeds. However, while these bodies of work address either security or reproducibility, there is a critical gap in systematically evaluating the impact of security hardening measures on the functional reproducibility of scientific workflows .The motivation for our work stems directly from this gap and the pressing need for a systematic, empirical evaluation of container security specifically within research domains. Each container image in our dataset was processed through a multi-stage experimental pipeline, depicted in Figure 1, designed to assess its initial security posture, apply hardening techniques, and subsequently evaluate both the security im-provements and the preservation of functional reproducibility. The pipeline would automatically trigger on code changes or updates to base images, build the container (ideally using multi-stage builds from minimal bases), perform vulnerability scanning, apply automated remediation where possible, re-scan, and execute reproducibility tests. The weekly package update baseline represents current practice in many research environments, while our multi-scanner approach provides enhanced security posture through systematic vulnerability detection and remediation. We have presented a novel reproducibility-aware DevSecOps framework that systematically addresses the critical tension between container security and scientific reproducibility in research environments. The framework’s key innovations include: (1) a multi-scanner vulnerability detection protocol that captures complementary security insights across different tools, (2) structured compara-tive analysis methods for evaluating security improvement approaches against operational baselines, and (3) nuanced reproducibility assessment protocols that account for domain-specific tolerances and acceptable scientific variations. This work contributes to the research software engineering community by providing: (1) a systematic methodology for balancing security and reproducibility concerns, (2) vali-dated protocols for multi-scanner vulnerability assessment, (3) structured approaches for comparative security analysis, and (4) complete open-source implementation of all framework components.

This is a desired property of diffusion pipelines, as it means that the pipeline can create a different random image every time it is run. In many cases, one would like to generate the exact same image of a certain run, for which case an instance of a PyTorch generator has to be passed: model_id = "google/ddpm-cifar10-32" # load model and scheduler # create a generator for reproducibility generator = torch.Generator(device="cpu").manual_seed(0) # run pipeline for just two steps and return numpy tensor image = ddim(num_inference_steps=2, output_type="np", generator=generator).images print(np.abs(image).sum()) Running the above always prints a value of 1491.1711 - also upon running it again because we define the generator object to be passed to all random functions of the pipeline. In short, one should not expect full reproducibility across different hardware when running pipelines on GPU as matrix multiplications are less deterministic on GPU than on CPU and diffusion pipelines tend to require a lot of matrix multiplications. Let’s see what we can do to keep the randomness within limits across To achieve maximum speed performance, it is recommended to create the generator directly on GPU when running model_id = "google/ddpm-cifar10-32" # load model and scheduler # create a generator for reproducibility generator = torch.Generator(device="cuda").manual_seed(0) # run pipeline for just two steps and return numpy tensor image = ddim(num_inference_steps=2, output_type="np", generator=generator).images print(np.abs(image).sum()) Running the above now prints a value of 1389.8634 - even though we’re using the exact same seed! The function is used everywhere inside the pipelines allowing the user to **always** pass a CPU generator even if the pipeline is run on GPU: model_id = "google/ddpm-cifar10-32" # load model and scheduler # create a generator for reproducibility # run pipeline for just two steps and return numpy tensor image = ddim(num_inference_steps=2, output_type="np", generator=generator).images print(np.abs(image).sum()) Running the above now prints a value of 1491.1713, much closer to the value of 1491.1711 when the pipeline is fully run on the CPU.
